name: The Opponent-Process Theory
statement: Colour is coded in opposing pairs, so we never see a reddish-green or a yellowish-blue.
statementAccent: we never see a reddish-green or a yellowish-blue
meaning: The opponent-process theory holds that colour perception is controlled by three opposing, or antagonistic, channels: red versus green, blue versus yellow, and black versus white, the last carrying light and dark. Each channel can signal one of its two colours or the other, but not both at once, so the colours in each pair are opponents that mutually exclude one another. This structure explains a striking fact of perception: we can see colours like reddish-yellow, orange, or bluish-green, but never a reddish-green or a yellowish-blue, because those would require a channel to signal both of its opposites simultaneously. It also explains negative afterimages, since staring at red fatigues the red-green channel and lets green dominate afterward. The theory was proposed by the German physiologist Ewald Hering in the late nineteenth century, in opposition to the trichromatic theory of Young and Helmholtz. Modern understanding reconciles the two: trichromacy describes the three cone types at the receptor level, while opponent processing describes how their signals are combined at a later neural stage.
mechanism: Opponent-process theory concerns how the signals from the cone photoreceptors are combined by later neurons. Rather than passing on the three cone responses unchanged, the visual system computes differences between them, producing opponent channels. A red-green channel compares the long-wavelength and medium-wavelength cone signals, a blue-yellow channel compares the short-wavelength cones against the sum of the others, and a black-white channel carries overall lightness. These channels are built by neurons, in the retinal ganglion cells and onward through the lateral geniculate nucleus, that are excited by one colour and inhibited by its opponent, for example excited by red and suppressed by green. Because a single channel can lean only one way at a time, the opposite colours of a pair cannot be seen together, which is why reddish-green and yellowish-blue never occur. Adapting one side of a channel, as by staring at red, shifts the balance so the opposite side dominates when the stimulus is removed, producing the complementary afterimage. This opponent stage sits atop the trichromatic receptor stage, so the two theories describe different levels of the same system rather than competing.

examples.text: We can see orange and teal but never a reddish-green or a yellowish-blue, because a channel cannot signal both of its opposites at once.
Staring at red fatigues the red-green channel, so on looking at white the green side dominates and a green afterimage appears.
Neurons in the retina and beyond are excited by one colour and inhibited by its opponent, building the red-green and blue-yellow channels.

variants.name: The three opponent channels
variants.text: Red-green, blue-yellow, and black-white, the antagonistic pairs that code colour and lightness.

variants.name: Reconciliation with trichromacy
variants.text: The modern view that trichromacy describes the cones and opponent processing describes the later combination of their signals, two stages of one system.

whyItMatters: The opponent-process theory is a cornerstone of modern colour vision science, explaining features of colour perception that the trichromatic theory alone cannot. It accounts for why certain colour combinations, reddish-green and yellowish-blue, are never experienced, for the complementary colours seen in negative afterimages, and for the way colours in simultaneous contrast shift toward the complement of their surroundings, all of which reflect the antagonistic channels. Historically, the theory, proposed by Ewald Hering, seemed to compete with the Young-Helmholtz trichromatic theory, but the two were reconciled into a two-stage model that is now standard: three cone types at the receptor level feed opponent channels at a later neural stage. This reconciliation is a classic example of how apparently rival scientific theories can describe different levels of the same process. The opponent-process framework guides research on the neural coding of colour, informs colour spaces and technology, and underlies the understanding of colour appearance. As the account of how cone signals become the opposing dimensions of colour, it is essential to the science of vision.

working.text: start from the responses of the three cone types at the receptor level.
have later neurons combine them into opponent channels, excited by one colour and inhibited by its opposite.
represent colour along red-green, blue-yellow, and black-white axes, so opposites exclude each other and afterimages appear in complements.

limits: The opponent-process theory describes the neural processing stage of colour vision and does not replace the trichromatic theory, which describes the receptor stage; the two are complementary stages of one system, and treating them as rivals is a historical misunderstanding now resolved. The exact correspondence between the perceptual opponent colours and the underlying neural channels is not perfectly simple, and the physiological channels do not map onto the pure red, green, blue, and yellow of perception in a one-to-one way, a subtlety still studied. The date of Hering's proposal is cited variously in the late nineteenth century, commonly 1892. So the opponent-process theory robustly explains the opposing structure of colour perception and its afterimages and contrasts, understood as the later stage that builds on trichromacy, with the precise neural-to-perceptual mapping an area of ongoing research.
misreadings: The opponent-process theory does not contradict trichromacy; the two describe different stages, cones at the receptor level and opponent channels at a later neural stage, and are combined in the modern account. It does not claim there are only four colours, but that colour is coded along opposing axes, which is why reddish-green cannot be seen. And the neural channels do not map perfectly onto the pure perceptual colours, so treating the theory as a rival to trichromacy, as limiting colours to four, or as a simple one-to-one code, misreads an account of how cone signals are combined into opposing dimensions of colour.
origin: Proposed by the German physiologist Ewald Hering in the late nineteenth century (commonly dated 1892), in opposition to the Young-Helmholtz trichromatic theory and later reconciled with it as a two-stage model.
